client: I've been really struggling since I failed my calculus final last month. It's like this constant voice in my head telling me I'm not smart enough to be in my major, that maybe I chose the wrong path entirely. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the grade is already there and it's not going away.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a quiet but persistent heaviness around this — that inner voice has really taken hold and turned one difficult grade into a question about your whole identity and future. You're right that the grade itself won't change, but what *can* shift is the story you're telling yourself about what it means, and that story is causing you a lot of pain right now. I'm curious — when that voice says you're "not smart enough," what evidence does it draw on, and is there anything it might be conveniently leaving out?

client: I guess the voice mostly just points to that grade, like it's this big glaring proof that I don't belong in the program. But when you ask what it's leaving out... I don't know, maybe the fact that I've done okay in other classes, or that my professor said my ideas were actually interesting even if the execution fell short. It's weird though, because even saying that out loud, I can kind of hear myself dismissing it already, like those things don't really count the same way the failure does.
therapist: It's really insightful that you noticed the dismissal happening in real time — that pattern actually has a name in CBT, "mental filtering," where our mind treats negative information as the only evidence that truly counts while discounting the positive. What's interesting is that you *can* hear the counterevidence — the other classes, your professor's feedback — it's just that your mind has set up an unequal weighing system where failures count as proof but successes get explained away. What do you think would need to be true for those positive pieces of evidence to feel just as "real" and valid as the failed exam?

client: I get what you're saying about the unequal weighing thing, and honestly it makes sense when you describe it like that. But I think the problem is that the failed exam feels more "real" because it has consequences — like, my grade is actually affected, my GPA could drop, that's tangible. The good feedback from my professor is just... words, you know? It doesn't undo the damage.
therapist: You're making a genuinely fair point — the grade does have real, tangible consequences, and it wouldn't be helpful to pretend otherwise. But I want to gently challenge one piece: you're framing your professor's feedback as "just words," yet the story that you don't belong in your major — the one causing you so much pain — is *also* just words, just thoughts, and somehow those feel very real and consequential too. It seems like your mind is applying very different standards depending on whether the "words" support the negative narrative or the positive one. What do you think it would look like to take the professor's feedback as seriously as the critical voice — not to cancel out the grade, but to sit alongside it as equally real?

client: That's... actually a really uncomfortable point, and I kind of hate that it makes sense. Like, I can see what you're doing — you're pointing out that I'm basically cherry-picking which "words" count as truth, and the ones that tear me down always win. But honestly, even understanding that doesn't make it feel easier to believe my professor over the voice in my head that's been telling me I don't belong here for years.
therapist: It makes complete sense that understanding something intellectually doesn't automatically make it *feel* true — that gap between knowing and believing is real, and it's actually one of the most human and frustrating parts of this kind of work. What strikes me is that you mentioned this voice has been there for *years*, which tells me it's had a lot of practice and repetition building its case, so it's not going to lose its grip just because we poked a hole in its logic once. I'm wondering — can you trace back to where that voice first started, or was there a moment earlier than this exam where it first told you that you didn't belong?

client: Yeah, actually... I think it goes back further than I usually let myself admit. There was this moment in middle school where I got into an advanced math class, and one of the other kids said something like "you only got in because they needed to fill spots" — and I remember laughing it off at the time, but something just... stuck. It's weird to say out loud because it sounds so small, like why would one comment from a twelve-year-old still be running my life, you know?
therapist: The fact that you can trace it back to that specific moment is really significant, and I want you to sit with something — a twelve-year-old's throwaway comment landed so deeply because it found a place where you were already vulnerable, already wondering if you truly belonged, and it's been quietly shaping your story ever since. It doesn't sound small at all; it sounds like the seed of a belief that's been growing for years, and your mind has been collecting evidence for it ever since — like that failed exam — while dismissing anything that contradicts it. What do you think that younger version of you actually needed to hear in that moment, that they didn't get?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think... that younger me needed someone to just say "you belong here, you're not invisible, and what you think matters" — but nobody did, and I'm not sure I even knew I needed that until right now. It's a little overwhelming to sit with that, because it makes me realize how long I've been carrying something I never even named.
therapist: What you just did takes real courage — naming something for the first time after carrying it silently for years is no small thing, and it makes sense that it feels a little overwhelming right now. What strikes me is that you just gave that younger version of you exactly what they needed, right here in this moment — you saw them, you named what they were missing, and you said it mattered. I'm wondering, as you sit with that realization, what it might feel like to slowly start offering that same voice — "you belong here, what you think matters" — to the version of you that's in your major right now?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it could work that way... but honestly, it feels almost too simple. Like, telling myself "you belong here" in the middle of a lecture where everyone else seems to just get it, while I'm sitting there completely lost — it feels kind of hollow, you know? I'm not sure a few words are going to undo years of feeling like I snuck in through a back door that wasn't meant for me.
therapist: That skepticism is actually really healthy and worth honoring — you're not looking for a magic phrase to paper over something deep, and that makes sense given how long this has been with you. What I'd gently push back on is the image you just used: "sneaking in through a back door" — because that framing assumes everyone else in that lecture belongs effortlessly and only you are faking it, when the reality is that feeling lost in a difficult class is often shared by many people who simply don't show it. I'm curious — when you look around that lecture hall and assume everyone else "just gets it," what are you actually seeing, and how much of that might be your mind filling in a story rather than reading the truth?

client: I mean, yeah, I see people typing notes, nodding along, maybe asking a question here and there — but I guess I don't actually know what's going on inside their heads. It's just that they look so calm and put-together, and I'm sitting there feeling like my heart is racing and I've lost the thread completely. I hear what you're saying about my mind filling in a story, but it's hard to believe it's just a story when the feeling of not belonging is so overwhelming and real.
therapist: You're touching on something really important — the feeling of not belonging is genuinely overwhelming and real, and I don't want to minimize that by reducing it to "just a story." But notice what you actually observed: people typing, nodding, asking questions — and then your mind added "therefore they understand and I don't," which is a conclusion, not something you saw. The racing heart, the lost feeling — those are real experiences, but they're also exactly what anxiety does, it floods your body with a sense of danger that feels like evidence even when it isn't. What do you think it would be like to experiment with separating the physical feeling from the conclusion — to notice "my heart is racing" without automatically letting it confirm the belief that you don't belong?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I get the logic of it — like, intellectually I can see that "people nodding" isn't the same as "they all get it and I never will." But in the moment, when my heart is pounding and I feel completely lost, it's like my body has already made the decision for me before my brain even gets a chance to weigh in. I'm not sure I can just... pause and label it when everything feels like it's happening so fast.
therapist: What you're describing is actually one of the most honest and accurate things you can say about anxiety — when your nervous system fires that fast, it genuinely does hijack the thinking brain before you have a chance to reason your way through it, so the goal isn't really to pause *in* the storm but to build enough familiarity with the pattern *before* it hits that your brain has a slightly faster chance of recognizing it. It's less like stopping a wave mid-crash and more like learning to notice the tide pulling back beforehand. I'm wondering — are there any moments, even small ones, where you've caught yourself mid-spiral and something shifted, even slightly?

client: I mean... maybe once or twice, like there was this one time I was spiraling about whether my coworker was mad at me for something I said in a meeting, and I remember catching myself thinking "wait, I've done this exact thing before and it was nothing." But honestly, even when I notice it, it doesn't really stop the feeling — it's like I can see the wave coming and I still get knocked over anyway. So I'm not sure if that counts as a shift or if I'm just watching myself suffer with slightly more awareness.
therapist: What you just described absolutely counts — in fact, it's more than you're giving yourself credit for, because you recognized a pattern mid-spiral and connected it to past experience, which is exactly the skill we're trying to build. "Watching yourself suffer with slightly more awareness" might sound like a small consolation, but that observer part of you is actually the doorway out — it can't stop the wave immediately, but over time that pause between trigger and conclusion gets wider and wider with practice. I'm curious, in that moment with your coworker, what happened after you caught yourself — did the spiral eventually lose some of its grip, even if it took a while?
